hooks: You can now count cost. What is the simplest structure to practise on, and what can two pointers do with it?
Sorted data lets you throw half away each step. How do you search that fast?
Binary search needs order. What if you want O(1) lookup with no order at all?
Hash maps find things fast but forget order. What if order is the whole point, like undo or a queue line?
Stacks and queues sit on a chain of nodes. What does a linked list cost you in pointers?
One pointer per node, one next. Give each node two children and what do you get?
Trees have one path between any two nodes. Allow cycles and many routes, and you need graph algorithms.
Graphs hide one more trick: solving a big problem by solving smaller copies. How does recursion do it?
dsa.upNext: Next, System Design: use these building blocks to decide how many servers, caches and queues a real product needs.

hooks: You have a framework. But how big is this system: requests per second, storage, bandwidth?
You know the load. One server will not carry it, so who spreads the traffic?
Servers are spread out and stateless. How do you stop every request from hitting the database?
A cache shields the database but does not replace it. How do you choose and scale the real store?
Some work is too slow for the request path. What can you hand off and finish later?
Queues and replicas mean copies drift apart. What do you promise readers about fresh data?
Consistent or not, one noisy client can still flatten you. How do you cap them at the door?
Everything is built. How do you see it failing before your users tell you?
system-design.upNext: Next, API Design: the contract that clients and services use to talk to the system you just sketched.

hooks: You can name resources and verbs. What does the server say back: 200, 404, or something worse?
Status codes give the category. Where does the detail of what went wrong go?
Errors tell the client what failed. But who is this client, and what may they do?
You know who is calling. What happens when they ask for a list of a million records?
Pages work. What happens when a client retries a payment because the reply was lost?
Retries are safe now. But how do you change the API without breaking current callers?
Versioning needs a source of truth. How do you write the contract down so both sides can check it?
OpenAPI describes REST well. When do gRPC, GraphQL or webhooks fit better?
api-design.upNext: Next, SQL Essentials: the queries and indexes behind every handler in your API.

hooks: You can read one table. But real data is split across many tables on purpose. Why?
Data lives in separate tables. How do you stitch it back together without duplicating rows?
Joined rows are only the start. How do you count, sum and group them into answers?
Grouping collapses rows. When a query gets tangled, how do you break it into readable steps?
What if you want a ranking or running total without collapsing the rows?
Your query is correct but takes 40 seconds. What lets the database skip most of the table?
You added an index. How do you check the database actually used it?
Fast and right, until two users write at once. What keeps the data safe?
sql.upNext: Next, Git and Collaboration: how a team safely changes the code that runs these queries.

hooks: You can commit locally. How does a team decide who branches from what, and when?
Branches diverge. When it is time to join them, do you merge or rebase?
Two people changed the same line. What does Git do, and what do you do?
Conflicts resolved. How does the change get reviewed before it lands on main?
It merged and broke production. How do you undo it without losing anyone's work?
Undo handles whole commits. What if you need one commit from elsewhere, or must find which one broke it?
You can move any change around. Who is allowed to, and what if a secret slipped into history?
git.upNext: Next, Software Testing: the checks that run on every pull request before it merges.

hooks: Most tests belong at the base. What does a good unit test look like?
Unit tests must stay isolated. How do you fake the database, the clock and the network?
You can fake dependencies. Does writing the test first change how you design them?
Mocks only prove your assumptions. Where do you test against a real database?
Real databases cover your own data layer. How do two services check they still agree?
Contracts cover the seams. What about the full user journey, and why does it flake?
You have many suites now. How much should you trust a green coverage number?
Coverage is easy on new code. How do you add tests to code nobody dares touch?
testing.upNext: Next, OOP and Design Patterns: how to shape code so it stays easy to test and change.

hooks: Classes bundle state and behaviour. But should you extend them or assemble them?
Composition keeps parts swappable. What rules keep a design from rotting as it grows?
SOLID says depend on abstractions. Who hands a class the things it depends on?
With dependencies injected, how do you control how objects get created?
Creating is solved. How do you wrap and connect objects that do not fit together?
Structure is set. How do objects talk to each other and change behaviour at runtime?
Patterns help, until they are overused. How do you spot code that is going bad?
You can smell and fix problems. Can you design a whole class model from a blank page?
oop-design-patterns.upNext: Next, Concurrency: what happens when many threads use these objects at the same time.

hooks: Concurrency is about structure. How do you actually run many tasks on a few threads?
Thread pools suit CPU work. When you mostly wait on I/O, why use an event loop instead?
Now many things run together and share data. What goes wrong when two touch it at once?
A race corrupts data. How do locks and semaphores stop it?
Locks fix races but can freeze the program. What is a deadlock?
Locks are costly. When can a single atomic operation do the job, and what is visibility?
Atomics are subtle. What if there is nothing shared to protect in the first place?
Pass messages, share nothing. Put it together: how do producers and consumers coordinate?
concurrency.upNext: Next, Web Fundamentals: the browser-to-server path where all of this runs under real traffic.

hooks: The page load opens a secure connection. How does the browser know the server is who it claims?
The channel is encrypted. What do the requests inside it actually say?
The same request is made a million times. How do browsers and CDNs avoid repeating it?
Caching treats every user the same. How does the server remember who you are?
Cookies tie a browser to a site. Why does the browser block calls to other origins?
CORS controls which sites may call you. How do you let another app act for a user?
Login is solved. What do attackers try against all of this?
Request and response is not the only model. How do you push live updates to the browser?
web-fundamentals.upNext: Next, put it to work: testing strategy, automation and security for a web app like this one.
